1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Piano
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5.background: One of the oldest recorded openings: Pedro Damiano recorded games in it at the beginning of the 16th century.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3.background: The name, Italian for "very quiet game", was given by Adolf Anderssen.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3.strategy: Defends e4 and prepares a slow, patient build-up: White avoids an immediate fight in the centre, keeps the tension, and plays for a manoeuvring game in which the centre is advanced only after careful preparation. The solid, modern way to play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3.strategy: Prepares to build a broad pawn centre by taking control of d4, so that the d-pawn can advance and stay there. It is the classical approach: White wants the centre first and the initiative later, accepting that Black will challenge it at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and defends e4, heading for a slow, symmetrical game. By delaying the central pawn moves White keeps its options open and sidesteps the sharper theory, but also gives up the quick grab of the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O.strategy: Gets the king safe first and decides on the central plan later: either the slow build-up with d3 or a central break at the right moment. Black gets a free choice of set-up in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4.strategy: Sacrifices a pawn to gain time: if Black takes, c3 comes with tempo on the bishop and d4 follows, building a big centre before Black is developed. White gets an initiative and open lines for the pawn; Black has to know the defence precisely.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d4.name: Italian Game: Rosentreter Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d4.strategy: Strikes at once, offering a pawn for quick development: more of Black's pieces already bear on d4 than White's, so the pawn is usually lost, and White hopes for a quick attack on f7. The gambit is not quite sound, so White must play accurately.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Bxf7+.name: Italian Game: Jerome Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Bxf7+.background: Named after Alonzo Wheeler Jerome of Paxton, Illinois, whose game with it against William Shinkman was published in the Dubuque Chess Journal in 1876. It was a brief fad in the late nineteenth century but is almost never seen today.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Bxf7+.strategy: Sacrifices a bishop, and soon a knight, for two pawns, hoping to expose the king for a mating attack. Black takes the pieces and defends, keeps a clear material advantage, and White has no real compensation.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Pianissimo, Normal
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it pressures e4, controls d5 and prepares castling. Black mirrors White's quiet set-up, so neither side commits the centre and the game is a patient fight over the right moment to open it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 f5.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Pianissimo, Lucchini Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 f5.background: Named after the Italian player Marco Lucchini.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 f5.strategy: A gambit that tries to turn a quiet position into a sharp one: the pawn attacks e4, but it also weakens f7 and the diagonal to the king. White can take the pawn or simply develop, and Black has to prove its compensation, which is doubtful.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 d6.strategy: Defends e5 and opens the c8-bishop, keeping the king's knight at home for the moment so that Black can still choose its set-up. Solid and flexible, though a shade more passive than developing the knight at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 f5 5.Ng.strategy: The sharp reply: the knight joins the bishop against f7, the square the f-pawn has left, where only the king defends it. White tests the weakened king at once, but Black has a good defence and White's edge is smaller than after simple development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 f5 5.ex.strategy: Takes the pawn, but ...d5 hits the bishop at once and Black regains the pawn with an open game while White is underdeveloped. The result is level, so accepting gives up the edge that simple development keeps.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 f5 5.Nc.strategy: Declines the pawn by simply developing: the knight guards e4, which the f-pawn attacks, and White keeps a solid position and a comfortable game. Black has loosened the king's side for no concrete gain and has to prove that the gambit works.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 f5 5.Ng.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Pianissimo, Dubois Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 f5 5.Ng.strategy: Blocks the bishop on c1 from g5, so the knight there loses its only defender and the queen attacks it. White can fork queen and rook with Nf7, but Black has sacrifices ready: this is the critical test of the gambit, and the one to learn.
Develops and covers h5, so there is no queen check, but it ignores the knight jump to f7: protected by the bishop, it forks queen and rook. Black loses material before the king's side is secure.
Defends f7 and eyes g5, but Bf7+ drives the king off its square: taking with the queen loses it to Nxf7. White keeps the initiative with the knight still on g5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 5.N.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Pianissimo, Italian Four Knights Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 5.N.strategy: Develops the knight and guards e4 a second time. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so White gives up the central pawn plan for fast piece play and the idea of pinning the knight on f6.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 5.c.strategy: Prepares the central break d4 at the right moment and gives the bishop the b3 retreat. White chooses a slow build-up over early confrontation: both sides keep solid pawn structures, and the game turns on manoeuvres.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 5.O.strategy: Castles first and settles the queenside set-up later. Nothing hangs, since the d-pawn guards e4. A flexible, solid choice that leaves Black free to decide on its own arrangement.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 5.B.strategy: Pins the knight against the queen at once. It adds pressure on f6, but Black can challenge the bishop with ...h6, and White has committed the bishop before the centre is clear.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 5.N.strategy: Mirrors White: the pawn defends e5 and opens the c8-bishop, keeping the position symmetrical and solid. Neither side has an obvious weakness, so the game turns on who finds the better squares for the pieces.
Completes kingside development before committing the d-pawn. It is sound, but with the d-pawn still at home White can take on e5 and fight for the centre with d4, so Black has to be ready for that.

Takes g5 from White's bishop before it can pin the knight, a precaution that costs a tempo and keeps Black flexible about castling. It is slower than developing but sound, and the d-pawn can still choose its square later.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 5.N.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Pianissimo, Canal Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 5.N.strategy: Pins the knight on f6 against the queen. That adds pressure on f6 and on the d5 square, where White's knight would like to land. Black normally challenges the bishop at once, so the pin is as much a question as a threat.

Castles and keeps the choice of set-up for later. This is the quiet route to a slow build-up in which both sides keep solid pawn structures, and the game turns on manoeuvres rather than early tactics.
Offers to trade the active bishop on c5. If Black takes, fxe3 gives White a half-open f-file and more control of d4 at the price of doubled pawns; if not, White can take the bishop itself.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6.name: Four Knights Game: Italian Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight with an attack on e4, which White's knight defends. The symmetrical structure leaves the centre unresolved and gives both sides a safe, flexible position from which to choose a plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 d6.strategy: Holds e5 and opens the c8-bishop but leaves the king's knight at home, so e4 is not challenged. White can then chase the bishop with the knight; the setup is solid but slow.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nge7.strategy: Brings the knight out without blocking the f-pawn, but it does nothing for f7, which only the king guards. Ng5 at once piles a second attacker on that square and puts Black on the defensive, and the knight puts no pressure on e4. White gets the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..strategy: Castles first and leaves the quiet pawn move for later; the knight on c3 covers e4, so nothing hangs. A flexible route to the same slow set-up, though the usual order puts the pawn move first.

Supports e4 with a pawn, so the knight on c3 is no longer tied to it, and opens the c1-bishop. White builds slowly with a solid structure, and the game becomes a long manoeuvring fight with a central break prepared piece by piece.
Grabs a pawn but loses a piece. After Nxe5, d4 seems to fork bishop and knight, but the knight takes the bishop first: ...Nxc4, and after dxc5 Black is a piece up for a pawn.
Supports e5 and frees the c8-bishop, mirroring White's solid set-up. Black delays castling to see how White develops, keeping the symmetrical structure and a flexible choice for the other pieces.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..strategy: Completes kingside development: both kings are safe and the structure is symmetrical. Black accepts that White will build up slowly, but nothing in the position is weak, and the fight is for the right time to play in the centre.

Takes b5 from the white bishop and gives its own bishop a retreat on a7 should White try to chase it. A useful waiting move that keeps Black flexible about castling, though it leaves the centre for later.
Takes the pawn, but White strikes first with Bxf7+: after Kxf7, Nxe4 regains the piece and attacks the bishop on c5, while Black's king has lost castling and stands exposed.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..background: The name Giuoco Pianissimo, "Very Quiet Game", was given by Adolf Anderssen.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..strategy: Supports the e4 pawn and opens the c1 bishop without committing to a central break. White chooses a slow build-up over an immediate d4: both sides have solid, symmetrical pawn structures, and the game is decided by manoeuvring and later pawn breaks rather than early tactics.

Fights for the centre at once. If the pawns are exchanged on e5 and Black recaptures, the queens can come off and the game simplifies, with little left for either side; White gives up the slow build-up for the quicker equal game.
Guards e4 with the rook, leaving the c3-knight and the d-pawn free for other jobs. Flexible, but White leaves the c1-bishop shut in behind the d-pawn and does not yet settle the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn, so the knight on c3 is no longer tied to it, and White heads for the slow build-up with both kings safe. A long manoeuvring middlegame follows, with a central break prepared piece by piece.
Grabs a pawn but loses a piece. After Nxe5, d4 seems to fork bishop and knight, but the knight takes the bishop first: ...Nxc4, and after dxc5 Black is a piece up for a pawn.
Guards e4 with the rook, leaving the c3-knight and the d-pawn free for other jobs. Flexible, but White leaves the c1-bishop shut in behind the d-pawn and does not yet settle the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, which nothing defends. White has to protect the pawn or give it up as a gambit, so Black takes the initiative while developing naturally.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O d6.strategy: Supports the e5 pawn with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop, a solid set-up that keeps the king's knight flexible. Black gives White the freer hand in the centre, since nothing yet challenges it, and accepts a patient, slightly passive game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Bb6.strategy: Moves the bishop out of reach of a later c3 and d4 while keeping its aim at f2, but the bishop was not yet under threat, so the move costs a tempo. It is safe and keeps the game level, though White can build the centre without hindrance.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn and keeps the position closed, heading for the slow set-up in which White prepares the central advance. The most patient way to meet the attack on e4.

Defends e4 with a piece rather than a pawn and develops at the same time. It reaches the symmetrical knight set-up with White already castled, which keeps the centre pawns flexible while e4 is guarded.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Albin Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..strategy: Prepares the central strike with a pawn and offers e4 as a gambit: if Black takes it, White strikes in the centre and gets a lead in development. If Black declines, White has a flexible set-up with the classical plan in reserve.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Deutz Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..background: The line has no standard name and has also been called the Max Lange Gambit.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..strategy: A gambit: the pawn attacks the bishop and e5, but Black can take it and trade the pieces that White's attack needs. White has open lines and quick development as compensation, but the pawn is real.

Supports e5 and opens the c8-bishop, the most natural set-up against the slow build-up. Black keeps the king in the centre for the moment and has flexible plans on both wings, with the bishop on c5 still pointing at f2.
Castles at once, completing kingside development and leaving the d-pawn free for a later central break. The king is safe, and Black waits to see which plan White chooses.
Takes g5 away from the white bishop so the knight on f6 cannot be pinned. A sensible precaution, but it spends a tempo on the kingside before the centre is settled and gives White time to regroup.
Stops White from expanding with b4 and takes space on the queenside, but it commits early: the b5 square is weakened and Black has spent a move on the wing before finishing development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo, with a5
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..strategy: Prepares the central advance, which the pawn on a5 does not hinder. The queenside pawn does give Black a way to harass the bishop if it retreats to b3, so White has to watch the bishop's retreat as the pawn centre grows.

Protects the e4 pawn with the rook and develops the rook without committing the c-pawn. It is flexible and safe, but it does nothing about Black's plan of gaining queenside space with the a-pawn, so White loses time against the central build-up.

Develops the queen's knight behind the d3 pawn, where it guards e4 and supports the knight on f3. The price is that it blocks the c1-bishop and leaves the pawn centre for later, so the move is sound but slower than the central build-up.
Prepares the central advance. This reaches the main set-up of the slow Italian: White builds a solid pawn centre first and plays for the break when the pieces stand well.

Develops the knight to a square where it guards e4 and eyes d5 and b5, a symmetrical set-up in which both sides develop at ease. It gives up the c3 pawn move and the central build-up that goes with it, so the game becomes a manoeuvring fight over piece placement.

Pins the f6-knight to the queen, a more active idea than the quiet build-up. Black can put the question to the bishop with a pawn move on the kingside, though, and the bishop then has to decide where to stand: the pin costs time and does not improve the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..strategy: Prepares the central advance. Black's extra h-pawn move has cost a tempo, so White can carry on building a solid centre without hurry.

Develops the knight to a natural square, where it guards e4 and eyes d5 and b5. The knight takes the c3 square from the pawn, so White gives up the pawn centre for piece play; the move is comfortable but less ambitious than the central build-up.

A flexible waiting move: the rook defends e4 and White decides later between a pawn centre and piece play. It is sound, but it does not make use of the tempo Black spent on h6, so White gets less from the position than with the central build-up.

Prepares the central break d4 with a pawn behind it: if Black takes on d4, the recapture with the c-pawn hits the bishop on c5 and leaves White a broad centre. It also gives the c4-bishop the b3 and c2 squares to retreat to. The price is time: this is a slow manoeuvring game.

Reaches a level, symmetrical middlegame: the knight guards e4 and eyes d5 and b5, and neither side has a structural trump. White trades the c3 pawn move for quick piece play, a game decided by manoeuvring rather than by a break in the centre.

Pins the f6-knight to the queen and gives White a more active set-up than the quiet build-up. Black can ask the bishop a question with a kingside pawn move, however, and the pin is more a nuisance than a threat, so White gains little for the time spent.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..background: The name Giuoco Pianissimo is credited to Adolf Anderssen.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..strategy: Strikes in the centre before White can build with d4, and the pawn attacks the c4-bishop with tempo. Black accepts an open game in return for active pieces and a share of the centre, while White has to decide how to resolve the tension and where the bishop belongs.

The standard answer to a slow build-up: the pawn holds e5 and frees the c8-bishop, and Black waits to see how White organises the d4 break. It is solid rather than ambitious, because it leaves White the choice of when to open the centre.

Takes b5 from White's pieces and gives the c5-bishop the a7 square, so a later b4 push cannot harass it. It is a useful waiting move, but it leaves the centre uncontested, and White can prepare the d4 break undisturbed.

The accurate way to take the gambit pawn: after the exchanges on d4 Black is a pawn up, having given the bishop for a knight. White's compensation is a lead in development and the initiative, so Black has to defend carefully, but the extra pawn is real and Black can steer for a simplified game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Max Lange Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..background: The Max Lange Attack, which follows with 6.e5, is named for the German master Max Lange, who suggested it in 1854.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..strategy: Takes the pawn with the e-pawn and allows the sharpest reply: e5 hits the knight with tempo and starts a heavily analysed attack on Black's king. Black keeps the extra pawn but has to find accurate defensive moves from the start, and White chooses the pace.

Takes the pawn with the knight, which leaves the king alone to guard f7: Nxe5 follows with the knight and the bishop both aimed there and a lead in development for White. Castling does not help, since Be3 then attacks the knight on d4 a second time.
Takes the bishop that took the pawn, but Black retakes at once, so White is a pawn down and the compensation has to come from piece activity and quick development.

Hits the bishop with a pawn, but the bishop simply retreats and Black keeps the extra pawn. White has no quick way to win the pawn back and little to show for it; taking the bishop with the knight gets far more.
Pins the f6-knight to the queen, but the bishop has left the c1-h6 diagonal and no longer guards b2: ...Bxb2 takes the pawn and attacks the rook on a1, so White also loses the exchange.

Recaptures with the knight, which lands on a strong central square supported by the e5 pawn, and Black keeps the pawn won on d4. The knight on f6 also attacks the unprotected e4 pawn, so White must show the compensation quickly.

Retakes with the pawn and keeps the extra pawn, but opens the game for White: e5 attacks the f6-knight at once, and Black's king is still in the centre. White gets the initiative, and recapturing with the knight is simpler and safer.
Grabs a second pawn, but White exchanges knights on c6 and Black must recapture, which leaves it a bishop down for just two pawns, with the king still in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Max Lange Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..strategy: The point of the gambit: the pawn attacks the knight at once and gains space, and White's lead in development with the bishop aimed at f7 pays for the missing pawn. White commits to a direct attack on the king; if Black parries it, the extra pawn counts.

Backs up the e4 pawn so that the knight cannot take it, and prepares to open the e-file. White does not force matters, though: Black keeps the extra pawn, and without the direct attack of the main idea the gambit offers less than it costs.

Pins the f6-knight to the queen and prepares to take it, which would give a developed bishop for a knight in return for pressure on the centre. Black keeps the extra pawn without having to face a direct attack, so White gets less than from the main idea.

The principled counterattack: the pawn hits the c4-bishop, so if White takes the knight Black takes the bishop in return. Black is then a pawn up, but White's rook check on the e-file, the pawn on f6 and Black's undeveloped kingside keep the play sharp and balanced.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Max Lange Attack, Spielmann Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6 5..strategy: Dodges the pawn and eyes e5 and f2, but f7 is now guarded by the king alone: the bishop sacrifice on f7 and then Ng5+ drive the king aside, and the queen takes the stranded knight. It needs more care than the natural defence.

Sidesteps the pawn into the centre, but nothing guards the knight: Qe2 attacks it at once, and with the e5 pawn cramping Black's kingside it cannot be held without losing material. The extra pawn does not make up for that.
